Notes on Sourdough
Sourdough bread is leavened by a starter, a fermented mixture of flour and water that contains wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria. The bacteria produce acids that give the bread its tangy flavor, while the yeast produces the gas that makes the dough rise.

Keeping a starter healthy is mostly a matter of routine. Feed it equal weights of flour and water once a day, keep it at room temperature, and discard part of it before each feeding so the acidity does not build up too much.
Hydration, the ratio of water to flour, has a large effect on the final loaf. A dough at 65 percent hydration is easy to shape and produces a tight crumb, while a dough at 80 percent hydration is sticky and difficult to handle but rewards the baker with large, irregular holes.

Long, cold fermentation in the refrigerator develops more flavor. Many bakers shape their loaves in the evening, let them proof overnight at four degrees Celsius, and bake them straight from the fridge the next morning.
Finally, bake hot and covered. A preheated cast iron pot traps steam during the first twenty minutes, which keeps the crust soft long enough for the loaf to expand fully before the crust sets and browns.
